title: Ops ownership cascade and SLO adoption sprint plan
body:
Purpose:
This doc captures a pragmatic sprint-based plan to cascade operations ownership down to feature teams while bootstrapping service-level objectives (SLOs) across model-serving surface areas. The emphasis is incremental, low-friction changes that create visible wins in 6–8 weeks and set up repeatable onboarding for the next 20 services.

Background & problem statement:
- Platform has grown quickly; SRE support bandwidth is limited and many feature teams rely on ad-hoc incident handling.
- We lack consistent SLO definitions and an ownership model that ties service-level promises to an ops contact and a measured error budget.
- This causes firefighting, unclear escalation, and surprise customer impact when model-serving capacity or latency regresses.

Primary goals (6–8 week horizon):
1) Define and publish a minimal SLO taxonomy for model-serving endpoints (latency, availability, correctness signals).
2) Run two parallel 3-week sprints with two pilot feature teams to validate onboarding and automation.
3) Establish an "ops ownership cascade": name an ops steward in each team, document runbook, and configure basic alert-to-pager flows.
4) Deliver dashboards and a lightweight SLO report template used during weekly reliability reviews.

Success metrics (what success looks like):
- 2 pilot services have production SLOs, error budgets wired, and documented runbooks within 8 weeks.
- Mean time to acknowledge (MTTA) for sev>2 incidents drops 20% for pilot services.
- Platform team time spent on reactive paging for covered services reduced by 30% measured over a 4-week window after rollout.

Scope (in-scope):
- Model serving HTTP endpoints and associated routing layers for the two pilot services.
- Basic SLO types: p95 latency for inference, availability (successful responses), and a simple correctness proxy (rate of model assertion failures or hallucination-detection signal where available).
- Pager escalation wiring to on-call aliases, runbook templates, and baseline dashboards.

Out of scope:
- Full multi-region failover automation and complex customer SLAs.
- Dedicated capacity contract changes.
- End-to-end customer-facing SLA docs.

Stakeholders & RACI summary:
- Platform-engineering (Asha Mehta) — A: program lead, produce templates and dashboards; runs onboarding sprints.
- Pilot feature teams — R: implement SLO configuration, own runbooks, provide ops steward.
- SRE on-call squad (Evan Park) — C/R: validate alerts and escalation paths; help triage playbook gaps.
- Observability (Maya Thompson) — R: construct dashboards and alert rules; instrument correctness metrics.
- Solutions Eng / CS (Priya Desai) — C: provide customer-impact context for tolerance decisions.

Roles & responsibilities (practical):
- Ops steward (feature team): named person who owns the runbook, is primary contact for the first 24 hours after incident, and tracks error budget burn.
- Platform SLO custodian: platform-engineering maintains the SLO monitoring infra and template definitions.
- SRE bridge lead: responsible for ensuring escalation is visible and for running initial war-room if error budget is exhaustively burned.

Pilot selection criteria (why these two):
- Medium traffic (representative load) but low customer blast radius so we can iterate fast.
- Teams with at least one engineer who can act as ops steward and has capacity for a 1.5 day/week sprint involvement.

Phased rollout & sprint plan (detailed):
Phase 0 — Prep (week -1 to 0) 
- Deliverables: SLO taxonomy doc (single page), runbook template, alert baseline checklist.
- Tasks: finalize SLO target proposals, instrument simple latency and availability metrics in metrics platform, create shared Confluence folder and slack channel (#ops-cascade).

Phase 1 — Pilot sprint A (weeks 1–3)
Week 1 (Discovery & instrument):
- Kickoff with pilot team A (1h): align scope, nominate ops steward.
- Platform: short spike to validate metrics emission and tagging (service_name, route, model_variant).
- Observability: create draft dashboard and sample alert rules targeting p95 and availability.

Week 2 (Configure & test):
- Feature team: add SLO config file to repo (small YAML) and deploy to staging.
- Platform: wire alert to team alias and platform on-call; create test alert fire drills.
- Runbook: feature team writes initial runbook draft (cause table, mitigation steps, owners).

Week 3 (Production roll & verification):
- Deploy to prod with SLO ruling enabled in passive mode for 48 hours (collect but don't page).
- Run simulated error budget burn test using traffic shaping or chaos injection in a controlled window.
- After post-mortem, flip to active paging for one non-critical rule.

Phase 2 — Pilot sprint B (weeks 4–6)
- Repeat Phase 1 pattern with pilot team B incorporating lessons from pilot A.
- Focus on correctness proxy metric instrumentation for team B (if available).

Phase 3 — Consolidation (week 7–8)
- Create an SLO adoption playbook from pilot artifacts.
- Host a 90-minute cross-team workshop to rehearse onboarding steps and share templates.
- Publish a prioritized backlog of automation items (e.g., SLO-as-code enforcement, runbook linting).

Sprint ceremonies & cadence:
- Twice-weekly 30-min sync between platform lead + pilot teams (Mon/Wed) during active sprints.
- Weekly reliability review where we show current error budget usage and outstanding work.
- Post-pilot retrospective to capture improvement actions and tooling gaps.

SLO taxonomy & example definitions (minimal viable):
1) Inference latency SLO (user-facing HTTP endpoints)
- Metric: p95 inference latency over 5m windows, measured at ingress proxy.
- Target: p95 < 220ms (measured as request end - request start), 30d rolling window for reporting; 7d lookback for alerting thresholds.
- Alert: sustained p95 > 300ms for 15 minutes -> page to team.

2) Availability SLO
- Metric: fraction of successful 2xx responses at endpoint excluding planned maintenance.
- Target: 99.9% over 30d rolling window (error budget 43.8 minutes per 30 days).
- Alert: drop below 99.7% on 1h window -> page.

3) Correctness proxy (MVP)
- Metric: model-assertion-failures / inference requests where assertion rules exist (or classifier-based hallucination score).
- Target: < 0.2% errors over 7d.
- Alert: > 0.5% for 30m -> page to feature team + models team.

Operational runbook template (fields to include):
- Service summary: what it does, owners, common dependencies.
- Known failure modes and previous incidents.
- Immediate mitigation steps (fast rollback, throttle, route to fallback model).
- Communication checklist (who to ping, customer templates).
- Post-incident actions and follow-up owners.

Instrumentation & automation backlog (initial items):
- SLO-as-code validation check in CI (block PR if SLO config missing).
- One-click dashboard bootstrap in observability console from template.
- Alert routing config generator to map service tags -> paging alias.
- Small SDK helper to emit correctness proxy when model runs inference (0.5d dev task).

Alerting & paging behavior guidelines (practical):
- Only page on clear actionable thresholds. Start conservative and refine.
- Use synthetic traffic to validate paging behavior before enabling production paging.
- For pilot services: page platform on-call + team ops steward for high-severity alerts.

Communications plan:
- #ops-cascade channel for live updates, runbook Q&A, and postmortems.
- Weekly reliability review notes published to Confluence.
- Customer-impactable incidents: draft message templates in Confluence, pre-approved by CS.

Onboarding checklist for feature teams (short):
1) Nominate ops steward and confirm availability.
2) Add SLO YAML to repo and run SLO-as-code linter.
3) Instrument latency/availability/correctness metrics with required tags.
4) Create runbook from template and link in service metadata.
5) Complete one paging fire drill and confirm pager fires to alias.
6) Present during weekly reliability review after 2 weeks live.

Observability signals & dashboards (minimal):
- SLO overview: error budget remaining, burn rate, last 30d performance.
- Latency heatmap by route + model_variant.
- Correctness trend with sample flagged traces.
- Recent paging events and MTTA/MTTR for the service.

Acceptance criteria for pilot completion:
- SLO metrics are visible on the shared dashboard and populated with 7+ days of data.
- Runbook exists and has been used in at least one simulated incident.
- Alert-to-pager path verified in a fire drill.
- Service owner signs off on SLO targets and runbook.

Risks & mitigations:
- Risk: Teams under-resource participation -> mitigate by time-boxing onboarding tasks and providing a small “fast path” automation bundle.
- Risk: Noisy alerts -> start with passive collection and iterate thresholds; add cooldown windows.
- Risk: Correctness metric not available -> provide a default lightweight assertion library and fallback to human review.

Next steps (first 2 weeks):
- Platform: publish single-page SLO taxonomy and YAML template (owner: Asha).
- Observability: create dashboard template and set up demo for pilot teams (owner: Maya).
- Run selection & kickoff: schedule pilot kickoff sessions and nominate ops stewards (owner: pilot team leads).

Appendix A — sample SLO YAML (MVP):
service: payments-infer
team: payments-platform
slos:
  - name: inference_latency_p95
    metric: p95_latency_ms
    target: 220
    window_days: 30
  - name: availability
    metric: success_ratio
    target: 99.9
    window_days: 30
  - name: correctness_proxy
    metric: assertion_failure_rate
    target: 0.2
    window_days: 7

Appendix B — 90 minute pilot workshop agenda:
- 0–10m: context and goals (platform lead)
- 10–25m: SLO taxonomy walkthrough and rationale (observability)
- 25–45m: hands-on: adding SLO YAML to service repo (pairing)
- 45–60m: runbook drafting exercise (split groups)
- 60–75m: alert test and fire drill planning
- 75–90m: next steps and Q&A

FAQ (quick):
Q: Who ultimately owns SLO targets?
A: Feature team owns the SLO for their service; platform provides guardrails and instrumentation.

Q: Will SRE block deployments based on SLOs?
A: Not generally. SRE may recommend rollout pauses if error budgets are exhausted; enforcement will be automated later through policy.

Q: Can we exempt internal-only endpoints?
A: Yes — add an exemption comment in the SLO YAML and file a short justification in the Confluence doc.

Notes & decisions log (living):
- 2026-02-10: program kickoff, taxonomy draft agreed (owner: Asha).
- 2026-02-18: pilot teams tentatively selected (payments-infer, search-rerank) pending steward confirmation.
